title: Classes
summary: **Classes** in TypeScript add static typing to JavaScript's class syntax: typed fields and methods, access modifiers (`public`/`private`/`protected`/`readonly`), constructor parameter properties, `implements`/`abstract` for contracts, `static` members, getters/setters, and true `#private` fields.

subtopics.title: Class fields and methods
subtopics.explanation: A class groups typed data (fields) and behavior (methods). Fields are declared with a name and type and may have initializers; methods are functions whose parameters and return types are checked. TypeScript verifies every field is assigned before use and that method calls match their signatures.

subtopics.title: Constructor parameter properties
subtopics.explanation: Prefixing a constructor parameter with an access modifier (public, private, protected, or readonly) declares and assigns a field in one step. This shorthand removes the boilerplate of declaring a field and then assigning this.x = x in the constructor body.

subtopics.title: Access modifiers
subtopics.explanation: public (default) members are accessible anywhere; private members only within the declaring class; protected members within the class and its subclasses. readonly allows assignment only at declaration or in the constructor. These are compile-time checks enforced by TypeScript, not runtime enforcement.

subtopics.title: Implementing interfaces
subtopics.explanation: A class can declare implements to promise it conforms to one or more interfaces. The compiler then checks the class provides every required member with compatible types. implements is purely a contract — it adds no behavior and is erased from the output.

subtopics.title: Abstract classes
subtopics.explanation: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and can declare abstract members that subclasses must implement, while also providing shared concrete code. It sits between an interface (pure contract) and a concrete class (full implementation).

subtopics.title: Static members
subtopics.explanation: static fields and methods belong to the class itself, not to instances. They are accessed via the class name and are useful for constants, factory methods, and shared counters that should not be duplicated per instance.

subtopics.title: Getters and setters
subtopics.explanation: Accessors let a property be backed by logic: a get runs when the property is read and a set when it is written, enabling validation or computed values while keeping property syntax. TypeScript infers the property type from the accessor signatures.

subtopics.title: # private fields vs private
subtopics.explanation: The TypeScript private keyword is a compile-time-only check, while ECMAScript #fields are truly private at runtime — inaccessible and even invisible from outside the class. Use # when you need hard runtime encapsulation; private is lighter and interoperates more easily with structural typing.

foundations.overview: TypeScript classes are JavaScript classes with a static type layer on top. You get typed fields, typed method signatures, and a family of class-only features — access modifiers, parameter properties, abstract members, and accessors — that the compiler enforces. Most of these annotations (modifiers, implements, abstract, types) are erased at compile time; the runtime behavior is plain JavaScript classes, with the exception of true #private fields which exist at runtime.
foundations.formalDefinition: A class is a blueprint defining the typed shape (fields), behavior (methods/accessors), and construction of objects. TypeScript layers compile-time visibility (public/private/protected), immutability (readonly), contracts (implements/abstract), and class-level members (static) over the ECMAScript class.
foundations.whyItMatters: Classes model stateful objects with encapsulation and inheritance, and are central to frameworks like Angular and NestJS and to many design patterns. Interviewers use them to probe understanding of encapsulation, the difference between compile-time and runtime privacy, and abstract-vs-interface decisions.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a class as a typed factory: the constructor builds instances with a known shape, modifiers control who may touch each member, and static members belong to the factory itself rather than the things it makes.
foundations.browserPerspective: Type annotations, access modifiers, implements, and abstract are erased during compilation — the browser runs ordinary ES classes. Only runtime features survive: #private fields, static members, and accessors. So compile-time privacy gives no runtime protection.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Service and component classes in Angular/NestJS, domain entities, view-model classes in state libraries, and small encapsulated utilities like a typed event bus or a cache wrapper.
foundations.businessImpact: Encapsulating invariants inside classes (via private state and validating setters) prevents illegal states from spreading through a codebase, reducing data-corruption bugs that reach users.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Access modifiers and abstract contracts let teams expose a small, safe surface and hide implementation details, so refactors of internals don't break callers.
foundations.performanceImpact: Negligible at runtime versus plain objects; class instances are standard JS objects. #private fields use a slightly different mechanism but the difference is immaterial for typical app code.
commonUseCases: Domain entities with validated state (private fields + setters)
Service/controller classes in Angular and NestJS
Abstract base classes sharing logic across subclasses
Static factory methods and shared constants

commonMisconceptions.myth: The private keyword prevents access at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: TypeScript's private is a compile-time check only and is erased; the field is still reachable at runtime (e.g. via bracket access). Use ECMAScript #fields for true runtime privacy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: implements adds behavior or code to a class.
commonMisconceptions.reality: implements is only a contract the compiler checks; it injects nothing and is erased from the output. You must still write every required member.

interactiveExamples.title: Parameter properties and access modifiers
interactiveExamples.explanation: Constructor parameter properties declare and assign fields in one line; private state is exposed only through methods. The sandbox strips types and runs the class as plain JS.

Use get celsius() to read it and set celsius(value) to validate before assigning.

debuggingLab.title: Mutating a readonly field
debuggingLab.symptom: Code tries to reassign an id field after construction and the compiler reports 'Cannot assign to id because it is a read-only property'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: readonly permits assignment only at declaration or inside the constructor. The reset method assigns this.id afterward, which violates the readonly contract, so the compiler rejects it.
commonMistakes: Marking identity fields readonly but then trying to mutate them.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Decide whether id should change. If it should, drop readonly; if it should not, return a new instance instead of mutating.

theory.question: What do TypeScript's access modifiers do, and which are enforced at runtime?
theory.directAnswer: public, private, and protected control where a member can be accessed: public anywhere, private only inside the declaring class, protected inside the class and its subclasses. readonly forbids reassignment after construction. All of these are compile-time checks that are erased from the output, so none of them are enforced at runtime — for true runtime privacy you must use ECMAScript #fields.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Keywords (public/private/protected/readonly) that constrain member visibility and mutability at the type level.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To express and enforce encapsulation — exposing a small intended surface and hiding internals.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler checks every access against the modifier and rejects violations; the keywords are then stripped, leaving plain JS with no enforcement.

theory.whyImportant: Mistaking compile-time privacy for runtime protection leads to security and encapsulation bugs; interviewers commonly probe this distinction.
theory.realWorldExample: A service exposes public methods but keeps its cache private so callers cannot corrupt internal state at compile time.

nestedTopics.title: readonly vs const
nestedTopics.explanation: readonly is a property modifier (no reassignment after init); const is for variable bindings.

nestedTopics.title: protected
nestedTopics.explanation: Accessible in subclasses, useful for shared internals in an inheritance hierarchy.

nestedTopics.title: Erasure
nestedTopics.explanation: Modifiers vanish at emit, so they offer no runtime guarantee.

followUps.question: How do you get true runtime privacy?
followUps.answer: Use ECMAScript #private fields, which are inaccessible and invisible outside the class even at runtime, unlike TypeScript's private.

followUps.question: Can you still reach a private field at runtime?
followUps.answer: Yes — since private is erased, the property exists on the object and is reachable (e.g. via bracket notation) in the emitted JS.

theory.question: When would you use an abstract class versus an interface?
theory.directAnswer: Use an interface when you only need to describe a contract with no shared implementation, and a class can implement many of them. Use an abstract class when subclasses should share concrete code or state in addition to a contract: it can hold implemented methods, fields, and a constructor while declaring abstract members that subclasses must provide. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one abstract class.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to define a contract: interfaces (pure, multiple) versus abstract classes (contract plus shared implementation, single inheritance).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Interfaces give flexible, implementation-free typing; abstract classes let you reuse common behavior across a related family of subclasses.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interfaces are erased and structural; abstract classes are real runtime constructs (minus the abstract keyword) that cannot be instantiated and may contain executable code.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrongly leads to rigid hierarchies or duplicated code; the trade-off is a classic OO design question.
theory.realWorldExample: A Shape abstract class implements describe() once and declares abstract area(); Circle and Square extend it and supply area().

nestedTopics.title: Single vs multiple
nestedTopics.explanation: One abstract base per class, but many interfaces.

nestedTopics.title: Shared state
nestedTopics.explanation: Abstract classes can hold fields and a constructor; interfaces cannot hold implementation.

followUps.question: Can an interface have method implementations?
followUps.answer: No — interfaces describe shape only and carry no implementation; if you need shared code, use an abstract class.

scenario.question: A class marks its balance field private, but a teammate reads account['balance'] in the compiled JS and a security reviewer flags it. How do you actually protect the field?
scenario.directAnswer: Explain that TypeScript's private is compile-time only and erased, so the field is reachable in the emitted JS. To make it truly private at runtime, switch to an ECMAScript #private field (#balance), which is inaccessible and invisible from outside the class. Expose access only through methods or a getter so the invariant is preserved at runtime, not just during type-checking.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Replacing compile-time-only private with runtime-enforced #fields to achieve real encapsulation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Sensitive state needs protection that survives compilation, which private does not provide.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: #fields are stored via a mechanism that throws on outside access and are not enumerable, so bracket access or inspection from outside the class fails at runtime.

scenario.whyImportant: Treating compile-time privacy as a security boundary is a real-world vulnerability; the fix demonstrates understanding of the runtime model.

nestedTopics.title: #fields semantics
nestedTopics.explanation: Hard-private, not reachable or enumerable from outside the declaring class.

nestedTopics.title: Interop trade-offs
nestedTopics.explanation: #fields don't participate in structural typing the way regular fields do, so mixing is intentional.

followUps.question: Does this fully secure secrets like tokens?
followUps.answer: It prevents accidental access, but anything in client-side JS can ultimately be inspected; true secrets must stay server-side, not just in #fields.

coding.question: Implement a Stack class with a private items array, typed push/pop, a size getter, and a static factory from(array) that builds a stack from an array.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want generic typing over the element type, a private field for the backing array so callers can't mutate it directly, push/pop with correct return types (pop is T | undefined), a size getter for read-only access to length, and a static factory that constructs and fills a new instance. Static methods belong to the class, so from is called as Stack.from(...).
coding.lineByLine: private items keeps the array hidden from callers. push appends; pop removes and returns T | undefined to reflect an empty stack. The size getter exposes length read-only. The static generic factory from<U> creates a new Stack, pushes each element, and returns it; it is called on the class itself, not an instance.
coding.timeComplexity: push/pop are O(1); from is O(n).

alternativeApproaches.title: #private items
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use #items for runtime privacy if callers must never reach the backing array even in compiled JS.
alternativeApproaches.code: class Stack<T> { #items: T[] = []; push(x: T) { this.#items.push(x); } }

followUps.question: Why make size a getter instead of a method?
followUps.answer: A getter exposes it with property syntax (s.size) and read-only access, signaling it's a derived, side-effect-free value.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Classes anchor object-oriented layers of frontend code: Angular/NestJS services and components, domain entities, and stateful utilities. Encapsulation via modifiers and abstract base classes lets teams expose a narrow public surface and centralize shared behavior.
productionDeepDive.performance: Class instances are ordinary JS objects with negligible overhead versus plain objects. #private fields use a distinct internal mechanism but the cost is immaterial for typical app workloads; favor clarity over micro-optimizing instance shape.
productionDeepDive.security: TypeScript private/protected are erased and provide no runtime protection — never rely on them to hide sensitive data. Use #fields for runtime encapsulation, and keep true secrets server-side since any client JS state is ultimately inspectable.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Abstract base classes and interfaces let many subclasses share contracts and logic without duplication, keeping large hierarchies consistent. Prefer composition over deep inheritance to avoid fragile, hard-to-change trees.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Use parameter properties to cut constructor boilerplate, validating setters to protect invariants, and meaningful access modifiers to document intent. Keep the public surface small so internal refactors don't ripple to callers.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI catches access-modifier and readonly violations before runtime. Combine with linting to flag accidental public exposure of fields meant to be private.

caseStudies.problem: Needed structured, dependency-injected services and components with clear public APIs and shared base behavior.
caseStudies.solution: Class-based architecture using access modifiers, parameter-property injection, abstract base classes, and decorators for metadata.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More ceremony than plain functions, but strong encapsulation and a consistent, tooling-friendly structure.
caseStudies.lessons: Classes shine when modeling stateful, contract-bound units; favor composition to avoid brittle deep inheritance.

keyTakeaways: TypeScript classes add typed fields, methods, and class-only features over ECMAScript classes; most type-level features are erased at runtime.
Constructor parameter properties declare and assign fields in one step, cutting boilerplate.
public/private/protected/readonly are compile-time checks only — use ECMAScript #fields for true runtime privacy.
Use interfaces for pure contracts (many per class) and abstract classes when subclasses share concrete code or state (one per class).
static members belong to the class itself; getters/setters back properties with validation or computed logic.
